topics.title: DRC v. Rwanda: New ICJ Genocide Case and the Limits of State Consent
topics.framing: The Democratic Republic of the Congo filed a new case against Rwanda at the International Court of Justice in June 2026, alleging acts of genocide and other atrocity crimes dating from 1996 to the present. Unlike the earlier 2002 case dismissed on jurisdictional grounds, Rwanda withdrew its reservation to ICJ jurisdiction under the Genocide Convention in 2008, removing a key hurdle. The case raises questions about the role of state consent in international adjudication and the ability of the ICJ to address mass atrocities.
topics.mainstream_view: Mainstream international law scholarship views the ICJ as a crucial forum for peaceful dispute resolution, and the DRC's new case as a legitimate exercise of treaty-based jurisdiction following Rwanda's withdrawal of its reservation. The earlier dismissal was a correct application of the consent principle, and the new case demonstrates the system's capacity to evolve as states accept broader jurisdiction. The focus is on procedural correctness and the ICJ's role in clarifying legal obligations under the Genocide Convention.
topics.global_south_view: TWAIL and Global South perspectives see the earlier dismissal as a failure of international law to protect African populations from mass atrocities, highlighting how jurisdictional reservations and state consent can shield powerful states from accountability. The new case is welcomed as a potential corrective, but skepticism remains about whether the ICJ, as a Western-centric institution, will deliver substantive justice for the DRC. The case also underscores the unequal power dynamics in international adjudication, where African states often bear the burden of proving harm while former colonial powers and regional hegemons evade responsibility.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides agree on the legal significance of Rwanda's reservation withdrawal, but diverge on whether the ICJ system adequately addresses historical injustices and power imbalances.

topics.title: Jamaica's Reparations Petition to the Privy Council: Colonial Legacies and International Law
topics.framing: On 7 September 2026, Jamaica formally presented a petition to King Charles III, as its head of state, requesting that he refer three questions about the legality of transatlantic chattel slavery and the UK's responsibility for reparations to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. This action is part of a broader CARICOM campaign for reparatory justice and follows years of grassroots mobilization. The petition seeks a legal reckoning with colonial-era atrocities and their ongoing legacies.
topics.mainstream_view: Mainstream legal analysis treats the petition as a novel but procedurally grounded use of the Privy Council's advisory jurisdiction, focusing on questions of historical legality and state responsibility. It is seen as a peaceful, rule-of-law-based mechanism to address longstanding grievances, potentially setting a precedent for other Commonwealth nations. The emphasis is on legal process, the role of the monarchy, and the possibility of negotiated settlements.
topics.global_south_view: TWAIL and Global South perspectives view the petition as a powerful challenge to the colonial legal order, using the very institutions of empire to expose their foundational injustices. They argue that slavery was always a crime against humanity, and that the petition is not just a legal tactic but a moral and political demand for truth, repair, and justice. The campaign is linked to broader Pan-African reparations movements, and the outcome is seen as a test of whether former colonial powers will acknowledge historical responsibility and engage in meaningful redress.
topics.convergence_note: While both recognize the petition's legal significance, mainstream views focus on procedural avenues, whereas Global South perspectives emphasize the need to overturn colonial legal frameworks and achieve substantive reparatory justice.

topics.title: Environmental Adjudication in the Anthropocene: TWAIL Perspectives on Unequal Harm
topics.framing: A recent TWAILR post examines environmental adjudication in the Anthropocene, arguing that legal imagination often manages unequal harm rather than challenging it. The piece highlights how inequality concerns both exposure to environmental harm and the power to define legal responses. This reflects a broader scholarly debate about the role of courts in addressing climate and environmental injustices, particularly in the Global South.
topics.mainstream_view: Mainstream environmental law scholarship sees adjudication as a key tool for advancing climate action, citing the growth of climate litigation globally, including in the Global South. Courts are viewed as capable of enforcing rights and holding governments and corporations accountable, with landmark cases in Pakistan, Colombia, and South Africa demonstrating progress. The focus is on the expansion of legal remedies and the potential for litigation to drive policy change.
topics.global_south_view: TWAIL scholars argue that environmental adjudication often operates within a legal framework that perpetuates colonial and neoliberal structures, managing harm rather than addressing root causes. They contend that the legal imagination is constrained by Western concepts of property and development, and that courts may reinforce unequal power relations. The emphasis is on the need for legal approaches that center the voices and experiences of marginalized communities and challenge the distribution of environmental harm.
topics.convergence_note: Both recognize the growing role of courts, but TWAIL critiques the underlying legal structures, while mainstream views see litigation as a progressive tool within existing frameworks.

topics.title: Deep Seabed Mining Disputes: Reviewability Gap in UNCLOS Article 189 and Investor-State Arbitration
topics.framing: In July 2026, the Seabed Disputes Chamber of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea issued provisional measures orders in the first contentious cases under Part XI of UNCLOS, brought by Nauru Ocean Resources and Tonga Offshore Mining Ltd against the International Seabed Authority. These cases highlight a reviewability gap under Article 189, which limits judicial review of the ISA's discretionary powers. The proceedings raise questions about the balance between regulatory authority and investor protection in deep seabed mining.
topics.mainstream_view: Mainstream international law and investment law perspectives view the SDC's orders as a necessary clarification of the legal framework for deep seabed mining, ensuring that the ISA's decisions are subject to some form of review while respecting its discretionary powers under Article 189. The cases are seen as a step toward legal certainty for investors and regulators, potentially reducing future disputes. The focus is on maintaining the integrity of the UNCLOS system and promoting responsible investment in the Area.
topics.global_south_view: TWAIL and Global South perspectives are concerned that investor-state arbitration and the SDC's review could undermine the ISA's regulatory authority and the principle of the common heritage of mankind. They argue that allowing private companies to challenge ISA decisions may prioritize commercial interests over environmental protection and equitable benefit-sharing. The reviewability gap is seen as a potential loophole for corporations to circumvent regulations, and there is skepticism about the neutrality of international tribunals in disputes between developing states and powerful mining interests.
topics.convergence_note: Both acknowledge the need for dispute resolution, but mainstream views emphasize investor protection and legal certainty, while Global South perspectives prioritize regulatory autonomy and the common heritage principle.

topics.title: ICC Prosecutor Removal and Institutional Legitimacy: Governance Challenges
topics.framing: On 24 July 2026, the Assembly of States Parties to the International Criminal Court voted to remove Prosecutor Karim Khan following disciplinary proceedings related to sexual misconduct allegations. The decision has sparked debate about the balance between institutional accountability and prosecutorial independence. Scholars are analyzing the governance implications and the legitimacy of the removal process.
topics.mainstream_view: Mainstream international criminal law scholarship views the removal as a necessary step to uphold the ICC's integrity and accountability, given the serious nature of the allegations. The process, including an independent external investigation and a secret ballot, is seen as reflecting the Assembly's role as the court's management oversight body. The focus is on strengthening internal governance mechanisms to protect the court's legitimacy and ensure a safe workplace.
topics.global_south_view: TWAIL and Global South perspectives are concerned that the removal process may be politically motivated, potentially undermining the independence of the ICC and its ability to pursue justice impartially. They argue that the Assembly's decision could set a precedent for states to interfere with prosecutorial functions, especially in cases involving powerful actors. There is also skepticism about whether the ICC's accountability mechanisms are applied consistently, given historical perceptions of the court's focus on African situations.
topics.convergence_note: Both agree on the need for accountability, but diverge on the risks to prosecutorial independence and the potential for political manipulation.

topics.title: Corporate Accountability in Ocean Governance: Legal Identity and Environmental Harm
topics.framing: A recent Opinio Juris piece examines corporate identity and accountability in ocean governance, focusing on how legal structures allow corporations to evade responsibility for environmental harm. This is part of broader discussions on flags of convenience, deep seabed mining, and the need for stronger international regulation. UN experts have also called for ocean governance to be grounded in international law, emphasizing business responsibilities.
topics.mainstream_view: Mainstream international law and policy perspectives acknowledge the challenges of corporate accountability in ocean governance, but see existing frameworks like UNCLOS and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights as providing a basis for progress. They emphasize the role of flag states and international cooperation in enforcing standards, and view corporate accountability as a matter of improving implementation and transparency. The focus is on incremental reforms within the current system.
topics.global_south_view: TWAIL and Global South perspectives argue that the current legal framework for ocean governance is skewed in favor of corporate interests, allowing flags of convenience and complex corporate structures to escape accountability. They contend that the 'common heritage of mankind' principle is undermined by neoliberal policies that prioritize profit over environmental and social justice. There is a call for a fundamental rethinking of legal personality and responsibility to ensure that corporations, particularly those from the Global North, are held accountable for harm caused in the Global South.
topics.convergence_note: Both recognize the problem of corporate accountability, but mainstream views favor technical fixes within existing law, while Global South perspectives demand structural changes to address power imbalances.
